title: Repeated loss of consciousness as the first symptom of recurrence of head and neck malignancy: a case report
case_prompt:
A 61-year-old man with a history of left lingual resection and left anterior cervical lymph node dissection followed by chemoradiotherapy for tongue cancer, and no prior syncope, was transferred two months after surgery for loss of consciousness.  
On admission:  
• Head MRI showed no cerebral infarction or metastatic tumour.  
• Electroencephalography was normal, ruling out epilepsy.  
• Transthoracic echocardiography revealed no structural heart disease.  
While hospitalized, after walking and after urination, he experienced sudden loss of consciousness lasting ∼30 minutes without prodromal symptoms. Continuous monitoring showed sinus arrest with junctional escape beats, followed by sustained sinus bradycardia for ∼20 minutes and concurrent hypotension, with recovery of consciousness as heart rate and blood pressure normalized.  
Orthostatic blood pressure testing (Shellong test) was normal. He was not taking any medications known to cause bradycardia.  
Given his surgical history, three reflex-syncope mechanisms were considered: carotid sinus syndrome, glossopharyngeal neuralgia syndrome, and parapharyngeal space lesions syncope syndrome. Carotid artery massage and cervical rotation–extension examinations revealed no abnormalities, and glossopharyngeal neuralgia was not observed. Therefore, parapharyngeal space lesions syncope syndrome was suspected.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Carotid sinus syndrome — excluded following provocative testing: “Carotid artery massage and cervical rotation-extension examinations revealed no abnormalities.”  
2. Glossopharyngeal neuralgia syndrome — excluded due to absence of characteristic pain: “Glossopharyngeal neuralgia was not observed.”  
3. Parapharyngeal space lesions syncope syndrome — favored because there was no known trigger and other causes were excluded: “Parapharyngeal space lesions syncope syndrome is caused by tumour invasion into the parapharyngeal space, and there is no known trigger for syncope.”
